introduction_markdown:
**Duration: three hours.** Enter the information required in the boxes of the flap. Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Inform the invigilator in case this booklet contains less than six questions, questions are repeated or there are blank pages so that the booklet should be changed. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^{3}\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. One atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed). Relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

The paper has three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6). All six questions are compulsory.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The mass spectrum of magnesium provides the following information:

| Isotopic mass | 24 | 25 | 26 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relative abundance | 0.79 | 0.10 | 0.11 |

(i) Define relative atomic mass.

(ii) Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Relative atomic mass.** The **relative atomic mass** of an element is the **weighted average mass of an atom of the element (taking into account the abundance of its isotopes), divided by one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12**. It is a ratio, so it has no units.

**(ii) Relative atomic mass of magnesium.** Weighted average of the isotopic masses:

$A_r = \dfrac{(24 \times 0.79) + (25 \times 0.10) + (26 \times 0.11)}{0.79 + 0.10 + 0.11}$

$A_r = \dfrac{18.96 + 2.50 + 2.86}{1.00} = \dfrac{24.32}{1.00} = 24.32$

**$A_r(\mathrm{Mg}) = 24.3$** (the abundances add up to 1.00).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Complete the table below by providing experimental evidence for the discovery of the following sub-atomic particles.

| Particle | Discovered by | Experimental Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Electron | J.J Thomson | |
| Neutron | Chadwick | |

*[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Particle | Discovered by | Experimental Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Electron | J.J Thomson | **Cathode-ray (discharge) tube experiment.** A beam (cathode rays) travelled from the cathode to the anode in a low-pressure gas. The beam was **deflected towards the positive plate** in an electric field and also deflected by a magnetic field, so it is made of **negatively charged particles**. The deflections gave the charge-to-mass ratio $e/m$, the same whatever the gas or cathode metal, so these particles (electrons) are common to all atoms. |
| Neutron | Chadwick | **Bombardment of beryllium with alpha particles** (from polonium) produced a highly penetrating radiation that was **not deflected by electric or magnetic fields (so it is neutral)**. It knocked protons out of paraffin wax (hydrogen-rich material), and from the energy of those protons the new particles were found to have a mass about equal to that of the proton: neutrons. |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Draw the dot and cross diagrams for each of the following species $\mathrm{BF_3}$ and $\mathrm{H_3O^{+}}$, stating their shapes.

$\mathrm{BF_3}$

$\mathrm{H_3O^{+}}$

(ii) Explain the reason for the similarity or difference in the shapes. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Dot and cross diagrams.** (Boron and oxygen electrons are shown as dots, the electrons of fluorine and hydrogen as crosses.)

**$\mathrm{BF_3}$.** Boron ($2,3$) has three outer electrons, each fluorine ($2,7$) has seven. Draw boron in the centre with its **three outer electrons (dots)**, each one paired with **one cross** from a fluorine atom to make **three single covalent bonds** (3 shared pairs). Each fluorine also carries **three lone pairs** (crosses), so each F has 8 electrons. The boron atom has only **6 electrons** in its outer shell (electron deficient, no lone pair).

**Shape of $\mathrm{BF_3}$: trigonal planar, bond angle $120^{\circ}$.**

**$\mathrm{H_3O^+}$.** Oxygen ($2,6$) has six outer electrons (dots). Draw oxygen in the centre, bonded to **three hydrogen atoms**: two bonds are normal covalent bonds (one dot from O and one cross from H each) and the **third is a dative (coordinate) bond** in which **both electrons come from a lone pair of oxygen** to the proton $\mathrm{H^+}$ (which has no electron). One **lone pair** (two dots) remains on oxygen. The whole ion is placed in square brackets with a charge of $+$ outside. Oxygen then has 8 electrons: 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair.

**Shape of $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$: trigonal pyramidal (pyramidal), bond angle about $107^{\circ}$.**

**(ii) Reason for the difference (valence shell electron pair repulsion, VSEPR).** Both species have **three atoms bonded to the central atom**, but their shapes **differ** because the central atoms have a different number of electron pairs:

- In $\mathrm{BF_3}$ the boron atom has **3 bonding pairs and no lone pair**. The three pairs repel equally and get as far apart as possible: a **planar triangle, $120^{\circ}$**.
- In $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ the oxygen atom has **3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair**, i.e. four electron pairs arranged tetrahedrally. The shape (describing only the atoms) is **pyramidal**. The lone pair is held closer to the nucleus and **repels the bonding pairs more strongly** than they repel one another (lone pair-bond pair repulsion greater than bond pair-bond pair repulsion), so the $\mathrm{H{-}O{-}H}$ angle is squeezed from $109.5^{\circ}$ to about $107^{\circ}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following results were obtained for the kinetic study of the catalysed reaction:

$\mathrm{A(g) + B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)}$

| Experiment no. | $[\mathrm{A(g)}]\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ | $[\mathrm{B(g)}]\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ | Initial rate/ $\mathrm{mol/dm^3/s}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | $1.2\times10^{-3}$ |
| 2 | 0.10 | 0.30 | $3.6\times10^{-3}$ |
| 3 | 0.20 | 0.10 | $2.4\times10^{-3}$ |

(i) Determine the order of the reaction with respect to

A:

B:

(ii) Determine the rate constant, K, stating its units

(iii) How would a catalyst affect the activation energy of the reaction? *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Orders of reaction** (compare two experiments in which only one concentration changes).

**A:** Experiments 1 and 3: $[\mathrm{B}]$ is constant ($0.10$) and $[\mathrm{A}]$ doubles ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.20$). The rate goes from $1.2\times10^{-3}$ to $2.4\times10^{-3}$, i.e. it also **doubles** ($2^x = 2$, so $x = 1$). The reaction is **first order with respect to A**.

**B:** Experiments 1 and 2: $[\mathrm{A}]$ is constant ($0.10$) and $[\mathrm{B}]$ is tripled ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.30$). The rate goes from $1.2\times10^{-3}$ to $3.6\times10^{-3}$, i.e. it is **tripled** ($3^y = 3$, so $y = 1$). The reaction is **first order with respect to B**.

Rate equation: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$ (overall second order).

**(ii) Rate constant** (experiment 1):

$k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]} = \dfrac{1.2\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}}{(0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})(0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})} = 0.12$

Units: $\dfrac{\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}}{\mathrm{mol^2\,dm^{-6}}} = \mathrm{dm^{3}\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

**$k = 0.12\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$** (the same value is obtained from experiments 2 and 3).

**(iii) Effect of a catalyst.** A catalyst **lowers the activation energy** by providing an **alternative reaction pathway (route) with a lower activation energy**. A larger fraction of molecules then has the energy needed to react, so the rate increases; the catalyst is not used up and does not change $\Delta H$ or the position of equilibrium.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Non-ideal solutions deviate positively or negatively from ideal behavior. Give two experimental evidences each to show how a mixture of:

(i) Ethanol and benzene deviate positively from Raoult's law.

(ii) Nitric acid and water deviate negatively from Raoult's law *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Ethanol and benzene (positive deviation).** The ethanol-benzene attractions are **weaker** than the ethanol-ethanol (hydrogen bonds) and benzene-benzene attractions, so the molecules escape more easily. Experimental evidence (any two):

1. The **vapour pressure of the mixture is higher than the value calculated from Raoult's law** (the vapour pressure-composition curve lies above the straight line of the ideal mixture).
2. The **mixing is endothermic** ($\Delta H_{\text{mix}} > 0$): the temperature of the mixture **falls** when the liquids are mixed.
3. The **volume increases** on mixing ($\Delta V_{\text{mix}} > 0$): the volume of the mixture is greater than the sum of the two volumes.
4. The mixture shows a **minimum boiling point azeotrope** (it boils at a lower temperature than either pure liquid and cannot be completely separated by fractional distillation).

**(ii) Nitric acid and water (negative deviation).** The $\mathrm{HNO_3}$-$\mathrm{H_2O}$ attractions (hydrogen bonding and ion-dipole interactions after ionisation) are **stronger** than in the pure liquids, so the molecules escape less easily. Experimental evidence (any two):

1. The **vapour pressure of the mixture is lower than the value predicted by Raoult's law** (the curve lies below the ideal line).
2. The **mixing is exothermic** ($\Delta H_{\text{mix}} < 0$): the mixture **becomes warm** (heat is evolved).
3. The **volume decreases** on mixing ($\Delta V_{\text{mix}} < 0$): the volume of the mixture is smaller than the sum of the two volumes.
4. The mixture forms a **maximum boiling point azeotrope** (about $68\ \%$ nitric acid, boiling at about $120^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$).
